text:
Lauren Bishop: Kicking off a thread to land on *tier names + semantics* for Dedicated throughput SLO. Sales is already asking “what are the tiers called?” and we need to align w/ Runtime + SRE on the actual guarantee.

Big open question: do we define the primary throughput guarantee in **tokens/sec** or **requests/sec**? My gut is tokens/sec, but want consensus + how we explain it to customers.

Draft PRD WIP here (pls comment inline): https://confluence.redwoodinference.com/display/PROD/Dedicated+Throughput+SLO+%2B+Tier+Definitions+%28Draft%29

Initial tier naming strawman: Standard / Performance / Premium. (Open to better names if these are too generic.)

—
Talia Benson: +1 on aligning fast. I’ve got a kickoff doc w/ questions if helpful, but agree we should pick primary metric + tier names this week so I can update the timeline. :thumbsup:

Sofia Ivanova: From runtime POV, req/sec is always going to be misleading unless you freeze prompt/response lengths + streaming behavior. Tokens/sec maps better to what’s actually saturating decode.

But we should be careful: *which* tokens/sec? output-only vs total (prefill+decode). If we guarantee “total tokens/sec” and a customer spikes prompt lengths, we get into weird fights.

Rafael Mendes: Agree w/ Sofia. SRE can operationalize tokens/sec as an SLI (rate over window), plus it’s easy to compute w/ standard exclusions.

For customer expectations: a lot of folks *ask* for “RPS”, but they actually mean “I need X throughput for typical prompt sizes.” We can offer an estimator in docs (“at 1k in / 200 out, expect ~Y req/s”) but keep the guarantee in tokens/sec.

Irene Choi: +1 tokens/sec. Also req/sec encourages “gaming” (tiny prompts) and doesn’t reflect fleet cost.

One more angle: tier names should map to shapes availability. If Premium implies H100-only, we need to be honest about regional supply constraints.

Jordan Blake: Sales perspective: customers absolutely say “requests/sec” and “concurrency.” If we show up with only tokens/sec, we need a super clean explanation + examples.

Could we define:
1) Contract/SLO primary metric = sustained output tokens/sec (with assumptions)
2) Sales sheet includes a table of “reference workloads” -> approximate req/sec

Also re: naming: Standard/Performance/Premium is fine, but “Premium” may trigger procurement scrutiny in enterprise (“why premium?”). Not a blocker.

Stephanie Nguyen: FWIW enablement wants names that are easy to pitch and don’t require caveats every sentence.

If we keep Standard/Performance/Premium, can we keep semantics really crisp?
- Standard: predictable sustained throughput, limited burst
- Performance: higher sustained + better tail latency guardrails
- Premium: highest sustained + most generous burst + strongest SLO credits

(But I defer to SRE/Runtime on what we can actually stand behind.)

Kira Thompson: For docs, tokens/sec is *fine* as long as we define it carefully and include a “how to think about it” section.

We should also explicitly call out streaming: customers see tokens trickle out. Their “throughput” perception = time-to-first-token + per-token rate. If we’re only guaranteeing decode rate over 5m, it won’t match what support gets ticketed on.

Lauren Bishop: Super helpful. Sounds like consensus forming: primary SLO metric = tokens/sec, but we need the customer-facing translation.

Sofia: on output-only vs total — I’m leaning output tokens/sec as primary. Prefill is too prompt-distribution dependent.

Rafael: what do you want for windowing? 1m vs 5m?

Sofia Ivanova: output-only tokens/sec is safest. We can add secondary metrics (prefill queue depth / TTFT) for dashboards + guardrails.

Window: operationally 1m is noisy; 5m smooths but may hide short pain. Maybe define SLO in 5m and alert on 1m burn? (SRE can weigh in.)

Rafael Mendes: Yep, that’s the usual pattern.

SLO: rate over 5m window, evaluated continuously.
Alerts: fast-burn on 1m, slow-burn on 30m/2h, etc.

Also: we should define *expected throttling* vs *SLO breach*. I’d rather throttle above committed concurrency than “breach” because customer overloaded. That belongs in tier semantics.

Irene Choi: +100. Fleet wise, we need admission control to protect the guarantee. Otherwise one noisy workload can crater the deployment and we get blamed.

Maybe each tier includes:
- committed sustained output tok/s
- committed max concurrent requests (or “committed concurrency envelope”)
- burst policy (duration + multiplier)

Jordan Blake: Re: “committed concurrency” — customers will ask “what if I don’t know my concurrency?” But we can frame it as: guarantee applies when traffic stays within your purchased envelope; above that we’ll *throttle* (not fail).

But we need to decide the wording so Sales doesn’t improvise.

Lukas Meyer: EMEA note: procurement/legal here prefer objective metrics + explicit carve-outs. Tokens/sec with a documented measurement standard is easier to defend than req/sec.

Also they’ll ask if we count input tokens. If we say output-only, we should be ready to explain why.

Lauren Bishop: OK, sounds like:
- Primary metric: **Sustained output tokens/sec** (per deployment) over 5m
- Customer-facing: provide “reference workload req/sec” table + guidance, but not contractually guaranteed
- Define concurrency envelope + throttling behavior per tier

Now tier names: any strong objections to Standard/Performance/Premium? Alternative suggestions?

Stephanie Nguyen: Not opposed. If we keep them, can we avoid “Premium = unlimited everything” perception? Like we should still have explicit burst ceilings.

Jordan Blake: No strong objections. Only request: don’t rename later. We’ve had whiplash before.

Irene Choi: Names are fine. Please just ensure the *shape mapping* is consistent:
- Standard: L4 / A10-class, maybe A100 (depending)
- Performance: A100/H100 (regional)
- Premium: H100 where available, plus stricter reservations

We can’t promise Premium in every region day 1.

Sofia Ivanova: No objections. Semantics matter more than names.

If we do “Performance” tier, I’d like to tie it to tail-latency guardrails and maybe disable some aggressive batching behaviors that increase p99. That’s runtime policy work, but doable.

Rafael Mendes: Agree. For SRE, tier definition must include what “overload mode” looks like:
- When we start throttling
- Whether we shed requests
- What error codes customers see
- How it shows up on dashboards

Otherwise Support will claim it’s an outage.

Kira Thompson: Action: I’ll draft the doc section “tokens/sec vs req/sec” w/ examples and what customers should measure on their side.

Also: can we standardize terms? “Sustained throughput” vs “Committed throughput” vs “Guaranteed throughput” — we should pick one to avoid mixed messaging.

Evelyn Hart: Joining late. I’m aligned with tokens/sec as primary. Please make sure the PRD includes:
- plain-English definition
- a customer example (“If you run chat prompts ~X in / Y out, expect ~Z req/s”)
- a clear boundary between *throttling* vs *breach*

Also: be conservative on what we call “Premium” until we’ve validated fleet supply.

Lauren Bishop: Great. Next steps:
1) I’ll update PRD by EOD w/ proposal: output tok/s primary metric + 5m window + concurrency envelope + throttle semantics.
2) Kira to draft customer-facing explainer section.
3) Rafael/Sofia: can you drop a quick comment in PRD re: windowing + which tokens/sec + alerting approach?

If no objections by tomorrow noon, we’ll lock tier names as Standard/Performance/Premium for v1.

(reactions: :thumbsup: from Talia Benson, Sofia Ivanova, Rafael Mendes, Jordan Blake; :eyes: from Stephanie Nguyen)
